title: A missing machine-parsed verdict defaults to the destructive answer
problem: My release gate was killed before it printed its decision, and because absence parses as failure, it threw away work that had already passed every check.
symptom: An iteration reverts with all gates green and no stated reason; the gate's log ends mid-verification.
why_now: Pessimistic defaults are correct for safety, but they are combined with writers that run under a hard timeout. The combination converts an interrupted decision into a destructive one, and no runtime distinguishes 'decided to revert' from 'never decided'.
existing: Pessimistic parsing: safe in isolation, unsafe when the writer can be killed.
Allowing a pending token: cures this failure and reintroduces premature reverts.
Longer timeouts: shift the cliff instead of removing it.

evidence.title: INC-0005: a killed step with no verdict token is read as reverted
evidence.quote: A machine-parsed verdict token that defaults to the destructive answer on absence is a critical safety hazard when its writer runs under a hard timeout.
evidence.note: Classified critical. Recorded fix is to write the verdict early on decisive evidence only and demote lower-priority audits to follow-ups.

build_hypothesis: Separate the two absences in the protocol: require an explicit decision record with a timestamp, and treat a missing record as INDETERMINATE (retry, preserve the tree) rather than as a revert.

check.manual_question: Your code parses a decision token and can revert. What happens when the token is MISSING because its writer was killed mid-decision: does absence read as 'revert' (destructive) or as 'indeterminate' (retry, preserve)?
check.rationale: A parsed verdict plus a destructive path is the exact combination that turns an interrupted decision into data loss. An explicit indeterminate state is the fix and it leaves a lexical trace.
